items.prompt: What is a wireframe in UX design?

options.label: A simple layout drawing showing where content sits on a screen
A finished visual design with final colours and images
A written report of the findings from user interviews
A coded version of the product that is ready to release

rubric: A wireframe is a low-fidelity layout of screen structure.
Distractors describe high-fidelity mock-ups, research reports or built products.

items.prompt: What does a user flow show?

options.label: The number of people who visit a website daily
The colour palette and fonts used in the product
The code structure behind each screen of the app
The steps a user takes to complete a task

rubric: A user flow maps the path a user takes to reach a goal.
Distractors confuse it with style guides, analytics or code architecture.

items.prompt: What is a prototype in UX design?

options.label: A written list of business goals agreed by stakeholders
A summary of all competitor products on the market
A final release that is live for every customer
A clickable model that simulates how a product works

rubric: A prototype is an interactive simulation used to test ideas.
Distractors describe goals documents, competitor analysis or a live release.

items.prompt: What is the main activity in a usability test?

options.label: Having the design team vote on which layout they prefer
Watching users attempt realistic tasks with the design
Asking users to rank the colour schemes they like most
Counting how many pages and links the site contains

rubric: Usability testing observes users doing tasks.
Distractors replace observation with opinion, counting or internal voting.

items.prompt: Which usability heuristic says the system should always keep users informed about what is going on?

options.label: Flexibility and efficiency of use
Help and documentation
Aesthetic and minimalist design
Visibility of system status

rubric: Visibility of system status covers feedback such as progress indicators.
Other options are real heuristics but address different ideas.

items.prompt: Which of the following are among Nielsen's usability heuristics? Select all that apply.

options.label: Error prevention
Hide advanced features from all users
Consistency and standards
Recognition rather than recall
Maximum animation on every screen

rubric: Consistency, error prevention and recognition over recall are established heuristics.
Animation overload and hiding features are not heuristics.

items.prompt: A design team ran a usability test on its prototype and found that three of five participants could not locate the search function. The team lead asks what the next step in the iterative design process is.

options.label: Ask developers to remove the search function entirely
Launch the product and wait for customer complaints
Stop testing because the design is now finished
Revise the design to fix the problem, then test again

rubric: Iterative design means revising based on findings and retesting.
Distractors skip iteration or end it prematurely.

items.prompt: Why do designers often start with low-fidelity wireframes instead of polished mock-ups?

options.label: Clients usually find designs easier to approve when they contain no content
Wireframes are cheap to change, so structure can be tested first
Wireframes are usually required by accessibility rules before any build starts
Polished mock-ups are too detailed for test participants to react to

rubric: Low fidelity makes changes fast and keeps focus on structure.
Distractors invent restrictions or requirements.

items.prompt: A breadcrumb trail such as Home > Shoes > Running shoes is best classified as which kind of interface element?

options.label: A decorative image that reinforces the brand
A navigation aid showing the user's location
A form input field for entering a search term
An error message telling users a page is missing

rubric: Breadcrumbs show location and help navigation.
Distractors misclassify it as another component type.

items.prompt: In a user flow diagram, a diamond shape usually represents what?

options.label: The entry point where a user first arrives in the product
The final step where a usability test session ends
A screen that holds a lot of content for the user
A decision point where the path can split

rubric: Diamonds conventionally mark decisions with branching paths.
Distractors misread the symbol as start, content or test end.

items.prompt: During testing, several participants cannot find a Save button. What is the most reasonable interpretation?

options.label: Users never need a Save button in any product
The test is invalid because it found a problem
The button likely needs to be more visible or better placed
The participants were careless and should be replaced

rubric: Repeated failures point to a design problem, not user fault.
Distractors blame users or dismiss the finding.

items.prompt: Why is it better to test a prototype before developers build the product?

options.label: Testing replaces the need for any later development
Problems are cheaper to fix before code is written
Prototypes always match the final product exactly
Developers are not allowed to read test results

rubric: Early testing avoids expensive rework.
Distractors overstate what testing or prototypes can do.

items.prompt: Why does placing buttons and menus consistently across screens improve usability? Select all that apply.

options.label: It removes the need for any user testing
Users learn the pattern once and reuse it
It reduces the effort of working out where to click
It makes every screen contain identical content

rubric: Consistency supports learning and lowers cognitive effort.
Consistent placement does not mean identical content or replace testing.

items.prompt: A checkout form asks for 12 fields, including optional ones like a second phone number. Analytics show many shoppers leave on this page. A designer proposes removing the optional fields. What is the reasoning behind this proposal?

options.label: Fewer fields make the page look more colourful
Less effort per step can lower the chance users give up
Shoppers prefer pages with no text on them
Optional fields are illegal to include in checkout forms

rubric: Reducing form effort reduces abandonment.
Distractors give irrelevant or false reasons.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a user flow in UX design?

options.label: To list every feature the business wants to build later
To record how many visitors a page receives each month
To map the steps a user takes to complete a task through a product
To define the colour palette and typography used across screens

rubric: A user flow maps the path a user follows to reach a goal.
Distractors confuse flows with visual style, analytics or feature backlogs.

items.prompt: Why do designers usually create low-fidelity wireframes before high-fidelity mockups?

options.label: Wireframes show how users react, so later usability testing of the design is not needed
Stakeholders approve colour and branding first, so wireframes just record those choices
Wireframes are detailed enough that developers can build from them without any mockups
Structure and layout can be changed cheaply before visual polish is added

rubric: Low-fidelity work keeps the cost of change low while structure is decided.
Distractors treat wireframes as final specs or as a replacement for testing.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the difference between usability and usefulness?

options.label: Usability is how a product looks and feels to users; usefulness is how quickly its pages and screens load
Usability is what designers judge from their own expertise; usefulness is what developers judge in code
Usability is how easily people use a product; usefulness is whether it meets a real need
Usability applies to mobile apps and their touch screens; usefulness applies to websites and their content

rubric: Usability concerns ease of use; usefulness concerns whether it serves a need.
Distractors mix up visual appeal, performance or who judges.

items.prompt: A usability test participant says nothing while struggling to find a button for a minute. How should the observer treat this behaviour?

options.label: As a sign the task was too easy for this participant and should be replaced with a harder one
As evidence of a usability problem, since the struggle shows the button is hard to find
As proof the participant is outside the target audience and their session should be discarded
As unreliable data, because the participant did not explain their thinking aloud

rubric: Observed behaviour is key usability evidence even without comments.
Distractors dismiss behaviour that is not spoken.

items.prompt: What does a clear visual hierarchy on a screen do for users?

options.label: Lets designers skip writing clear labels because users infer each button's purpose from its colour and size
Guides attention to the key elements first through size, contrast and position
Reduces the number of screens in a flow by merging separate steps into a single page automatically
Makes every element equally prominent so that users notice all the options and nothing is missed

rubric: Hierarchy directs attention by emphasising what matters.
Distractors claim equal prominence or that it replaces labels or flow design.

items.prompt: Which of the following are typical goals of a usability test? Select all that apply.

options.label: Measuring the company's total market share
Finding where users get stuck or make errors
Seeing whether users can complete key tasks
Proving that the team's preferred design is best

rubric: Usability tests reveal obstacles and task success.
Distractors describe confirmation bias and market research.

items.prompt: A designer shows a clickable prototype of a booking app to five users. Three of them tap the 'Save' icon expecting to confirm their booking, but it only bookmarks the venue. The designer wonders what this pattern means.

options.label: The prototype is too low-fidelity, so users cannot be expected to understand any icon in it
Those three users were careless, so their taps should be ignored and the icon kept as is
The booking button needs a brighter colour so users notice it before the Save icon
The icon's meaning does not match what users expect, so the icon or label is misleading

rubric: Repeated same mistake signals a mismatch between icon and expectation.
Distractors blame users or unrelated visual or fidelity factors.

items.prompt: You are designing a checkout flow. Users are abandoning at a form that asks for 15 fields, including optional ones. Which change best applies the principle of reducing user effort?

options.label: Defer optional fields until after purchase so only essentials appear
Rewrite the form heading and helper text in a friendlier, more reassuring tone
Add a progress bar showing the steps left but keep all 15 fields required
Shrink the font and spacing so all 15 fields fit on a single screen

rubric: Cutting nonessential fields reduces effort directly.
Distractors add cosmetic changes without lowering the work required.

items.prompt: A wireframe for a mobile recipe app must let users find a recipe, view it and save it. Which sequence of screens best matches this task flow?

options.label: Saved list, search results, recipe detail with a Save action, saved confirmation
Search results, recipe detail with a Save action, saved confirmation
Account creation, search results, recipe detail, saved list with a Save action
Search results, saved confirmation, recipe detail with a Save action, saved list

rubric: The shortest path follows find, view, save.
Distractors add unrelated steps or wrong order.

items.prompt: A form shows the error 'Invalid input' in red after users submit. Applying good error-message guidelines, which rewrite is best?

options.label: 'You made a mistake, please check every field again' in a bigger red font at the top
'Something went wrong on our side, please try again later' as a popup
'Error 4012: email validation failure' shown in a banner at the top of the page
'Use the format name@example.com' next to the email field

rubric: Good errors are specific, placed near the problem and say how to fix it.
Distractors are vague, technical or blame the user.

items.prompt: Five test participants each try a new navigation menu. Four cannot find 'Billing' under 'Account'; they look under 'Settings'. What is the most appropriate next iteration?

options.label: Leave the menu as is, since one of five participants found Billing
Keep the menu and add a tutorial pop-up explaining where Billing is
Rename 'Settings' to 'Account' everywhere and ship it without retesting
Cross-link Billing under Settings, then retest with new participants

rubric: Align structure with users' mental model, then retest.
Distractors patch with instructions, ignore the data or skip validation.

items.prompt: You must place a primary 'Pay now' button and a secondary 'Cancel' link on a payment screen. Which treatment applies visual hierarchy correctly?

options.label: Give both the same size and colour so neither action is favoured over the other
Make 'Pay now' a filled, high-contrast button and 'Cancel' a plain text link
Make 'Cancel' a filled, high-contrast button and 'Pay now' a plain text link
Make both filled buttons, with 'Cancel' in a brighter colour so it is easy to spot

rubric: Primary action gets the strongest emphasis; secondary gets less.
Distractors flatten or invert the hierarchy.

items.prompt: You are making a mobile screen easier to use with one thumb. Which changes apply that goal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Make tap targets large enough to hit accurately
Place frequent actions within the lower, easy-to-reach area
Shrink buttons to fit more on screen
Put the main action in the top corner away from the thumb

rubric: Reachable placement and adequate target size support one-handed use.
Distractors make reaching and tapping harder.

items.prompt: A designer tests a sign-up prototype with six users. Task times are fine, but five say they were unsure whether their account had been created after tapping 'Submit', since the screen just reloaded. The designer must revise the flow.

options.label: Shorten the form by removing optional fields so sign-up feels quicker to finish
Make the Submit button larger and brighter so users notice where to tap it
Add a tooltip over the form's fields explaining why each one is needed
Show a confirmation message that the account was created and what comes next

rubric: Visible feedback on system status resolves the uncertainty.
Distractors do not provide feedback or worsen the flow.

items.prompt: A shop's checkout has six steps: sign in, cart review, shipping, delivery method, payment, confirmation. Analytics show most abandoning users are first-time buyers purchasing one item. Which change best applies a flow-simplification rule for them?

options.label: Keep all six steps but add a progress bar, so users see how many screens remain before they can pay
Allow guest checkout with shipping and payment on one page, then offer account creation after purchase
Move payment to the first step, so users commit to buying before they enter any shipping information
Require account creation at the start, so saved details make later purchases shorter for every customer

rubric: Guest checkout removes steps that first-time, single-item buyers do not need while keeping the task intact.
A progress bar or reordering leaves the unnecessary steps in place; forced accounts add friction for new buyers.

items.prompt: In a usability test of a reporting tool, 4 of 5 participants could not find the 'Export' function, which sits in a three-dot menu. The team moves it to a visible labelled button in the toolbar. What is the correct next step in the iteration cycle?

options.label: Survey existing users on whether they like the new button, since opinions show whether it works
Run another round with new participants on the same task to check whether the change fixed the failure
Add a tooltip to the old menu as well, so both placements get tested together in one later round
Ship the change, since four of five failures already prove the earlier placement was the problem

rubric: Iteration means retesting the revised design on the same task with fresh participants to confirm the fix.
Shipping unverified or collecting opinions replaces observed task performance with assumption.

items.prompt: You are designing the main action, 'Book appointment', on a phone app that people mostly use one-handed while walking. Applying Fitts's law and thumb-reach guidance, which placement fits best?

options.label: A full-width, large button fixed at the bottom of the screen, within easy thumb reach
A small text link in the top-left corner, where the app title and menu already sit by convention
A large button in the centre of the page header, so it is the first element read on every screen
A medium icon at the top-right, where it stays visible while the page content scrolls underneath

rubric: Large targets near the thumb zone are faster and easier to hit one-handed.
Top corners are hardest to reach on a phone, and small targets raise error rates.

items.prompt: You must write a task for a usability test of a hotel booking site, to see whether users can find the cancellation terms. Which task wording follows good practice?

options.label: You're booking a room for May but your plans may change. Find out whether you could get a refund
Use the site's filter to show only hotels with free cancellation, then pick whichever one you prefer
Look at the hotel page and tell us whether the cancellation policy is easy to find and understand
Click on the 'Cancellation policy' link at the bottom of the hotel page and tell us what you think

rubric: A realistic goal without naming interface elements lets you observe whether users find the information themselves.
Naming the link or asking for opinions leads the participant and hides real navigation behaviour.

items.prompt: A sign-up form validates the password only after submission and then shows 'Invalid input' in a red banner at the top of a long page. Which redesign correctly applies error-handling guidelines?

options.label: Show a popup after submission listing every rule, which users must dismiss before retrying the form
Show an inline message next to the field saying what to change, such as 'Use at least 8 characters'
Keep the banner but make it larger and bolder, so it cannot be missed once the form reloads
Add a help page on password rules and link it from the banner, so users can read the rules in full

rubric: Inline, specific messages next to the field tell users what went wrong and how to fix it.
Generic banners, popups and external help pages separate the message from the field and add effort.

items.prompt: You are fixing a checkout form so that it is accessible to users with low vision and colour blindness. Which changes apply accessibility guidelines correctly? Select all that apply.

options.label: Link each visible label to its input so it stays on screen while typing
Show error states with an icon and text, not red colour alone
Keep light grey hint text, since hints are secondary content
Raise body text contrast against its background to at least 4.5:1
Replace visible labels with placeholder text to reduce clutter

rubric: Redundant cues, adequate contrast and persistent labels support these users.
Placeholder-only labels disappear on typing, and low-contrast hints are still unreadable to low-vision users.

items.prompt: Research shows the key task for a utility app's users is paying the monthly bill quickly. Today the path is: log in, dashboard, 'Billing' menu, bill list, choose bill, enter card, confirm. You are asked to redraw the user flow to serve that task. Which flow does it best?

options.label: Log in, a settings screen to store a card, dashboard, then the existing billing menu and bill list
Log in, dashboard with a 'Pay bill' card showing the amount due, confirm using the saved card
Log in, dashboard, 'Billing' menu with the bill list sorted by date, then the existing steps as before
Log in, dashboard with a banner linking to a billing tutorial, then the existing bill list and card steps

rubric: Surfacing the primary task on the first screen with prefilled details cuts steps toward the goal.
Other options keep the long path or add steps without shortening the main task.

items.prompt: A heatmap of a product page shows many clicks on a decorative product photo that is not clickable, while the real 'Details' link gets few. What is the most likely cause to analyse and act on?

options.label: Users dislike the photo, so they click on it to try to dismiss it before reading other content
The photo looks interactive and the link looks like plain text, so the affordances mislead users
The page loads too slowly, so users click repeatedly on the first element they see on the screen
The heatmap tool is miscounting clicks, so the pattern should be ignored until more data arrives

rubric: Clicks on non-interactive items alongside ignored links point to false and weak affordances.
Other options assume causes the pattern does not indicate, such as speed, dislike or tool error.

items.prompt: Analytics show 45% of users leave an onboarding flow at step 3. Session recordings show most of them stop at a system prompt asking for location access, before any explanation of why the app needs it. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The progress indicator is unclear, so users cannot tell how many onboarding steps are still left
Users at step 3 are not the target audience, so the drop-off is expected and needs no change
Step 3 contains too many form fields, so users give up on the flow because of typing effort
The permission is requested without context, so users distrust it and leave rather than decide

rubric: Recordings tie the drop-off to a context-free permission request that erodes trust.
Other options ignore the observed behaviour at the prompt and blame form length, progress or audience.

items.prompt: In testing, participants complete 'Send invoice' but take long and several say afterwards, 'I'm not sure it actually went through.' Which heuristic violation best explains this?

options.label: Flexibility and efficiency: there is no keyboard shortcut that experienced users could use to send faster
Visibility of system status: there is no clear confirmation that the action succeeded after sending
Consistency and standards: the send button uses a different colour from buttons elsewhere in the product
Error prevention: the form lets users enter invalid email addresses before they press the send button

rubric: Doubt after completing an action signals missing feedback about system status.
The other heuristics concern different problems and do not explain uncertainty after the send.

items.prompt: An A/B test of a pricing page shows variant B ('Start free, no card needed') has 30% more clicks on its button than A, but paid conversions are lower. Which analysis best explains the pattern?

options.label: Variant B's button is poorly positioned, so fewer people can find it and fewer of them go on to pay
Click counts are the true success measure, so variant B won and the conversion drop is only random noise
Variant B attracts less-committed visitors, and the promise differs from what the next screens ask for
Variant A must have a bug, because a variant with fewer clicks should never produce more paid conversions

rubric: Higher clicks with lower paid conversion suggests an expectation mismatch or lower-intent traffic further down the funnel.
Other options contradict the data (B has more clicks) or dismiss the conversion metric.

items.prompt: A tree test of a new site structure shows 80% of participants eventually reach the right page for 'find parental leave policy', but only 35% get there without backtracking. What does this most likely indicate?

options.label: The task was too easy, so the study should be repeated with harder tasks that spread results more
The final page title is wrong, because users would otherwise have found it directly on their first try
Participants did not read the task properly, so their paths say nothing about the structure itself
Two top-level labels both seem plausible for the content, so users guess a path and then correct it

rubric: High eventual success with low directness suggests ambiguous or overlapping labels at upper levels.
The other options attribute the pattern to task difficulty, the page title or participant carelessness without evidence.

items.prompt: Across five usability sessions on an intranet, which observations point to an information architecture problem rather than a visual design problem? Select all that apply.

options.label: One user misreads the grey disabled state of a button as an error
Several users open the same wrong top-level menu first for different tasks
Users say 'I'd have looked under Benefits, not HR forms' about the same page
Users repeatedly move between two sections looking for the same document
Two users miss the search button because its icon has low contrast

rubric: Wrong first clicks, mismatched mental models and back-and-forth between sections show categories or labels fail users.
Low-contrast icons and disabled-state misreads are visual presentation issues.

items.prompt: A redesigned booking flow passed lab testing with 90% task success, yet support tickets about booking rose after launch. The lab group was recruited from loyal customers and followed scripted tasks with a facilitator nearby. Which analysis best explains the gap?

options.label: The redesign must be reverted, since any rise in tickets proves that lab testing results are invalid
The support team probably changed its ticket categories, so the rise reflects reporting and not usability
The lab sample was familiar with the brand and guided, so first-time users' problems stayed hidden
Lab success rates are always inflated by about the same amount, so the results should simply be reduced

rubric: Loyal, facilitated participants with scripted tasks hide the difficulties of new users in real conditions.
The other options jump to reversal, assume a reporting change, or invent a constant correction.

items.prompt: In a moderated usability test, 4 of 5 participants failed to find the "Export" action, which sits in an overflow menu. In the post-task questionnaire, all five rated finding it "easy". What is the best reading of this?

options.label: The questionnaire and the observation cancel out, so the finding is inconclusive until a larger sample is tested.
The ratings outweigh the failures, because participants know their own experience better than an observer does.
The failures came from unusual task wording rather than the design, so the menu location is fine and the ratings confirm it.
Observed behaviour outweighs self-report, which is prone to politeness bias, so discoverability is a problem.

rubric: Behaviour observed in a task is stronger evidence than self-report, which is prone to bias and rationalisation.
Distractors trust self-report or dismiss a clear 4-of-5 pattern without evidence.

items.prompt: Analytics show checkout drop-off at the shipping-address step is 41% on mobile and 12% on desktop. The form and copy are identical. Which analysis step is most likely to locate the cause?

options.label: Rewrite the shipping page copy, since a gap this large usually means mobile users read the wording differently.
Run a desktop-only A/B test of the form layout, since the desktop result is the stable baseline for comparison.
Compare mobile and desktop field errors, keyboard types and time per field to find where friction differs.
Add a progress bar to both versions, since drop-off at a funnel step usually means users lack orientation.

rubric: The difference between platforms with identical content points to platform-specific interaction friction, which field-level data can reveal.
Distractors change content or layout without diagnosing, or ignore the mobile-specific symptom.

items.prompt: A card sort shows most users group "Invoices" with "Account", while the navigation puts it under "Settings". A tree test of the current navigation shows only 28% success finding invoices. What do these results together indicate?

options.label: Users need training on the Settings area, so a tooltip tour would fix the low success rate.
The nav's category structure conflicts with users' mental model, so the problem is grouping, not visual styling.
The tree test is unreliable because it removes visual design, so the card sort should be ignored here.
The label "Invoices" is unfamiliar to users, so renaming it should raise tree-test success on its own.

rubric: Card sort reveals expected grouping; low tree-test success confirms the mismatch lies in the hierarchy.
Distractors blame the label, the method or user knowledge, though the card sort shows users understand the term.

items.prompt: A redesigned landing page raised clicks on the main call-to-action by 35%, yet completed sign-ups fell by 8%. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: Clicks are the true success measure here, so the sign-up fall is random noise that the team can safely ignore.
The larger button is now so prominent that users stop scanning the page and skip the content that would have persuaded them.
The new button copy over-promises, so clicks come from users who hit unexpected requirements and leave.
The redesign changed the sign-up form's layout and length, so the form alone must account for the drop, whatever the clicks did.

rubric: A rise in clicks with a fall in completions suggests a expectation mismatch between the promise and the next step.
Distractors dismiss the funnel's end metric or assume unsupported causes.

items.prompt: In a think-aloud test of a prototype with an icon-only bottom navigation, participants complete tasks but pause for several seconds before each tap and say "I think this one is... settings?". What does this pattern most suggest?

options.label: Task success shows the navigation works, so hesitation is a normal cost of any interface.
The icons are too small, so enlarging tap targets alone will remove the hesitation.
Participants lack motivation, so the pauses reflect the test setting rather than the design.
Icons demand recall, not recognition, so adding labels should cut hesitation.

rubric: Hesitation with guessed meanings signals ambiguous icons; labels support recognition over recall.
Distractors treat success as proof of usability or attribute the cause to size or motivation.

items.prompt: A test of a help-centre redesign produced several observations. Which of them point to an information-architecture problem rather than a visual-design problem? Select all that apply.

options.label: Users find the right article quickly but say the grey text is hard to read.
Users open several wrong categories before finding the right article.
Users search by their own wording because no category label matches their term.
Users locate the search box immediately but mis-click on a low-contrast button.
Users in a tree test choose different top-level categories for the same task.

rubric: Wrong-path browsing, split category choices and label mismatch show structure and labelling problems.
Readability and contrast are visual-design issues, not structural.

items.prompt: A team tests an onboarding flow with a six-screen tutorial before the main app. Testers who skip the tutorial fail to create a project. Testers who read every screen also fail to create a project, and several say they "forgot it by then". The team proposes making the tutorial unskippable. What is the most accurate diagnosis?

options.label: Skipping is the root cause, so making the tutorial unskippable will fix creation failures for most testers.
The project-creation step has weak visual hierarchy, so a larger, higher-contrast button would fix both groups' failures.
The tutorial teaches too early and out of context, so guidance should move into project creation.
The tutorial is too short to be retained, so adding more screens would help users remember the steps.

rubric: Both groups failing shows the tutorial is not the lever; learning in context beats front-loaded instruction.
Distractors assume more or forced tutorial content helps, or blame an unrelated detail.

items.prompt: Users of a notes app delete notes often, usually on purpose, and rarely regret it. Notes can be restored technically. Criteria: keep the flow fast, prevent costly accidents, avoid dialog fatigue. Which design is best?

options.label: Delete immediately and show a brief undo toast, since reversibility makes a blocking confirmation unnecessary.
Show a confirmation modal every time, since any destructive action needs an explicit confirmation step.
Disable deletion for notes edited recently, since protecting new content matters more than speed.
Hide delete inside a menu to cut accidents, since fewer taps to delete cause more mistakes overall.

rubric: Undo meets all three criteria: fast, recoverable and no fatigue from repeated modals.
Distractors favour blanket confirmation or friction that violates the speed and fatigue criteria.

items.prompt: A team ran a 5-person moderated test of two checkout designs. Four preferred design B. The lead says this "statistically proves" B will raise conversion and wants to ship. Which critique is most valid?

options.label: The claim is sound, since four of five is an 80% preference, which is well above chance and a strong enough signal to ship.
The sample size is fine for this claim, but the test should have used unmoderated sessions to remove facilitator effects on preference.
Five participants can reveal usability problems but not support a statistical claim about conversion; run an A/B test.
The result would be valid only if all five participants had been existing customers, since new users can't judge a checkout flow reliably.

rubric: Small qualitative samples find problems; they don't estimate effect sizes or conversion lift.
Distractors accept the preference as proof or suggest irrelevant fixes.

items.prompt: A test found four issues. Rank by priority using frequency, impact on task completion and workaround availability. Which should be fixed first?

options.label: Seen by 4 of 6 users, blocks account creation, no workaround exists.
Seen by 1 of 6 users, caused data loss, but this user took an unusual path.
Seen by 3 of 6 users, a cosmetic misalignment that nobody commented on.
Seen by 6 of 6 users, a confusing label, easily worked around by trying again.

rubric: It combines high frequency, task-blocking impact and no workaround, so it ranks highest on stated criteria.
Distractors over-weight frequency alone, a rare edge case or a cosmetic problem.

items.prompt: A banking app has four destinations that users visit daily and switch between often. Criteria: one-tap switching, constant visibility of current location, thumb reach. Which navigation pattern is best?

options.label: A gesture-only swipe between sections, since it removes all visible controls and speeds switching.
A top-of-screen tab bar, since tabs near the title are easier to scan than lower ones.
A hamburger drawer at top left, since it saves screen space and scales to future destinations.
A bottom tab bar with four labelled tabs, since it keeps all destinations visible and in thumb reach.

rubric: Bottom tabs meet visibility, one-tap and reach criteria for a small, frequently used set.
Hamburger hides destinations; top tabs are poor for reach; gestures hurt discoverability.

items.prompt: An online shop has 3,000 products. Shoppers compare items, open details and return to the list at their previous place. Criteria: preserve position on return, support comparing, allow reaching the footer. Which pattern is best?

options.label: Infinite scroll with no state saved, since continuous loading reduces effort and raises engagement.
A single page loading all 3,000 products, since this removes any need to track position.
Pagination with persisted page and filters, since it keeps position and gives a reachable footer.
Infinite scroll with a footer fixed to the screen, since this makes the footer always reachable.

rubric: Pagination with preserved state satisfies position, comparison and footer criteria.
Distractors ignore return-position loss, performance, or use a workaround that harms the layout.

items.prompt: A team plans to test a concept using a polished, pixel-perfect high-fidelity prototype with early-stage ideas. Which are valid critiques of this plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: Participants may critique colours and polish instead of the underlying concept.
High fidelity makes it costly to discard or radically change a flawed idea.
High-fidelity prototypes are unusable for testing, so only paper works.
Participants cannot give feedback on flows at any fidelity level.
Polish may signal a finished decision, so participants hold back honest criticism.

rubric: High fidelity shifts feedback to surface detail, raises sunk cost and signals finality.
The other options overstate: flows can be tested at any fidelity, and hi-fi prototypes are testable.

items.prompt: A team has two weeks before launch of a redesigned checkout. A stakeholder wants to skip usability testing because the design follows best practice. The budget allows about three days of research. Criteria: lower launch risk, respect the deadline, focus effort where failure is costly. What is the best recommendation?

options.label: Delay launch until a full A/B test finishes, since only statistical evidence is acceptable for a redesign.
Test the whole product with twenty users, since broad coverage reduces risk more than focused tests.
Skip testing and monitor analytics after launch, since best-practice designs rarely fail in real use.
Run quick moderated tests of five users on the checkout's riskiest steps, then fix blocking issues before launch.

rubric: Small focused tests on the riskiest flow fit the time and budget while reducing launch risk.
Distractors ignore the cost of failure, the time budget, or the proportion of effort.

items.prompt: A team tested a checkout redesign with 5 participants and all 5 completed the purchase unaided. The product manager states the redesign has a task success rate of at least 95%. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Five successes support only a lower bound near 50 to 60 percent, so the 95 percent claim outruns the evidence.
The claim holds if participants were representative, since representative samples make intervals unnecessary.
The claim is invalid only because usability tests need at least 20 participants before any rate is reported.
The claim holds because zero failures in the sample means the true failure rate must be below five percent.

rubric: With n=5 and no failures, the confidence interval's lower bound is only about 50-60%, so a 95% claim is unsupported.
Distractors confuse zero observed failures with zero true failures, or treat representativeness as a substitute for statistical uncertainty.

items.prompt: An A/B test of a redesigned home page shows a 12% lift in click-through in week one, shrinking to 2% by week four, with returning users driving the decay. Which interpretation best fits the evidence?

options.label: The lift is largely a novelty effect, so judge on the stabilised returning-user effect and extend the test.
The week-one lift is the true effect, because early data comes from the largest and freshest pool of users.
The design harms returning users and should be reverted, because a shrinking lift always signals damage.
The test is invalid and must be discarded, because any change in effect over time shows randomisation failed.

rubric: Decay concentrated in returning users is the classic signature of a novelty effect, so the stabilised effect should drive the decision.
Distractors treat early data as authoritative, blame randomisation, or read decay as active harm.

items.prompt: Two weeks before launching an update to a banking app's transfer flow, a team has two usability specialists, no recruiting budget, and wants to catch the most severe issues. Judged against these criteria, which method fits best?

options.label: One specialist's review alone, because independent reviewers duplicate findings and slow a tight schedule.
A large unmoderated benchmark study, because it gives statistically reliable task times for the new flow.
Independent heuristic evaluations by both specialists, merged and severity-rated, accepting some domain gaps.
A satisfaction survey of existing customers, because it reaches many people quickly with no recruiting cost.

rubric: Independent heuristic evaluations need no participants, fit the timeline, and surface severe issues; merging reviewers improves coverage.
Distractors choose methods that need recruiting or budget, answer a different question (satisfaction, benchmarks), or discard the benefit of multiple evaluators.

items.prompt: An open card sort with 30 participants produces clear groupings. A designer proposes using them directly as the site navigation with no further checks. Which critique is best?

options.label: Open card sorts are unreliable below 100 participants, so the groupings should be discarded and the sort repeated.
The groupings are sufficient, because user-generated categories guarantee that people will locate content in the structure.
The groupings should give way to the organisation's internal chart, because stakeholder alignment outweighs user models.
Groupings reveal mental models but not findability, so validate the labels and hierarchy with a tree test on real tasks.

rubric: Card sorts show how people categorise, not whether they can find items in a proposed hierarchy; tree testing checks that.
Distractors overstate the sample requirement, assume categories guarantee findability, or replace user evidence with internal structure.

items.prompt: A usability study reports a SUS score of 80, above the commonly cited average of 68, yet 4 of 10 participants failed the critical task of cancelling an order. Which judgement should drive the next step?

options.label: Dismiss the failures as participant error, because the same participants rated the product highly afterwards.
Ship as is, because a SUS score above 68 shows overall usability is acceptable and failures are normal variation.
Rerun the questionnaire with a larger sample first, because only a stable average score can justify any design change to a flow.
Prioritise fixing the cancellation flow, because failure on a critical task outweighs a satisfaction score.

rubric: Observed failure on a critical task is high-severity behavioural evidence that a global self-report score can mask.
Distractors let an aggregate score override task-level evidence or blame participants.

items.prompt: A team replaces an 'Are you sure?' delete dialog with immediate deletion plus a 10-second Undo. Which are valid reasons this can be the better design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Undo removes any need to retain deleted data on the server for a short period.
Undo keeps the common, intended deletions fast and uninterrupted.
Confirmation dialogs are often dismissed by habit, so they protect users less than they appear to.
Undo is equally safe for irreversible actions such as sending a payment.
Undo lets users recover after noticing a mistake, which a pre-action dialog cannot support.

rubric: Habituation, post-hoc recovery and speed for intended actions are the established arguments for undo over confirmation.
Undo needs retained data for the window and cannot cover truly irreversible actions.

items.prompt: A subscription app's growth lead proposes moving the cancel option behind three screens and a retention offer, projecting 15% fewer cancellations. Support tickets about cancelling are already rising. Judged against long-term trust, regulatory risk and revenue, which response is best?

options.label: Keep cancel easy to find and test one optional retention offer, tracking cancellations, re-subscription and complaints.
Reject any retention offer, because presenting alternatives at the moment of cancelling is always manipulative.
Approve it, because retention offers are standard practice and fewer cancellations directly raise recurring revenue.
Approve it only for new subscribers, because existing users already know where cancellation used to be.

rubric: An optional offer with easy exit balances revenue against trust and regulatory risk, and the proposed metrics capture long-term effects.
Distractors accept an obstructive dark pattern or reject legitimate offers outright.

items.prompt: You have 12 participants to compare two navigation structures. Individual differences in skill are large, so you need within-person comparisons, and learning effects from repeated tasks must be controlled. Which plan meets every constraint?

options.label: Six participants use only A and six only B, then compare mean task times with no further controls.
Every participant uses A first, then B, with identical tasks, since a fixed order keeps conditions comparable.
Every participant uses both structures, with order counterbalanced and two equivalent task sets rotated across structures.
Every participant uses both structures in random order with identical tasks, relying on randomisation to cancel learning.

rubric: Counterbalanced order with parallel task sets gives within-person comparison while controlling order and task-learning effects.
Distractors fix the order, drop the within-person design, or reuse identical tasks so learning contaminates the second condition.

items.prompt: A data-analysis tool serves both first-time users and daily experts. The onboarding must not block experts, must help novices at the moment they need it, and must be recoverable if dismissed. Which design meets all three?

options.label: A skippable short start with hints on first use of each feature, and a way to reopen help later.
A mandatory seven-step tour for everyone, so all users share the same baseline before the interface unlocks.
A dense reference page linked from the footer, so experts are never interrupted and novices can read everything.
Separate simple and advanced editions chosen at signup, with no way to switch once the choice is made.

rubric: Skippable, contextual, re-openable help satisfies non-blocking, point-of-need and recoverable constraints together.
Distractors block experts, offer no point-of-need support, or lock users into a choice.

items.prompt: A team proposes a one-page mobile payment flow with inline card validation, a clear total and a wallet option. Constraints: users are often on unstable connections, and a payment must never be lost or charged twice. What is the design missing?

options.label: A promotional banner above the total, so basket value rises before connections drop mid-flow.
Extra optional profile fields on the page, so support can contact users whose payments fail.
Handling for interrupted submissions: kept entries, a visible pending state and retries that cannot double-charge.
A tooltip beside every card field explaining the expected format, because validation errors are the main risk on unstable connections.

rubric: Unstable connections require state preservation, clear pending status and idempotent retries to prevent loss or duplicate charges.
Distractors add content or help that does not address interrupted submissions.

items.prompt: You must define success measures for a site-search redesign. They must reflect users actually finding what they need, resist being gamed by clutter or confusing results, and connect to business outcomes. Which set meets these constraints?

options.label: Searches per user and average session length, tracked against repeat visits as the business outcome, since heavy use signals trust.
Result click-through rate, with results per page as a guardrail, tracked against ad revenue, since clicks show relevance.
Task success on seeded queries, with reformulation and zero-result rates as guardrails, tracked against downstream conversion.
Average session length and pages viewed per visit, with bounce rate as a guardrail, tracked against overall site traffic.

rubric: Task success paired with guardrail behaviours and a downstream outcome measures finding, not activity, and resists gaming.
Distractors use activity metrics that rise when search is worse (more clicks, longer sessions, more searches).

items.prompt: Design a date-of-birth input for a global product. It must support keyboard and screen-reader entry, dates decades in the past, and unfamiliar locale formats without ambiguity such as 03/04. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: A native date input, because browsers localise its format and show the chosen date in the user's own locale order.
Three dropdowns in the order the user's locale expects, with year listed newest first so users can scroll to their year.
A typed field accepting several formats, echoing the parsed date with the month spelled out, plus an optional calendar.
A calendar-grid picker with month and year arrows, which most users already recognise and which shows weekdays for context.

rubric: Flexible typed entry with an unambiguous echo supports accessibility, distant dates and locale ambiguity.
Distractors make distant dates tedious, impose one locale order, or leave ambiguity unchecked.

items.prompt: You are planning a usability test of a prototype nurses will use to calculate medication doses. Errors can harm patients, and real use is rushed and interrupted. Which elements must the test plan include? Select all that apply.

options.label: Participants who are practising nurses rather than colleagues.
Satisfaction ratings only, to avoid stressing participants.
Interruptions and time pressure built into the tasks.
Realistic edge-case scenarios such as unit mismatches and out-of-range doses.
A polished visual style, so reactions reflect the final product.

rubric: Safety-critical validity needs edge cases, realistic interruption and time pressure, and representative users.
Satisfaction-only measures miss errors, and visual polish is not required to test dose-calculation safety.

items.prompt: A claims tool used daily by 2,000 trained staff confuses new hires. Leadership wants better learnability but forbids retraining downtime and any drop in experienced staff throughput. Which rollout plan meets both constraints?

options.label: Build a separate simplified tool for new hires and keep experienced staff on the old one, then compare error rates between the two groups each quarter.
Ship an opt-in layout that keeps existing shortcuts, track throughput by cohort, and expand once experts match baseline.
Replace the interface for everyone at once with a design that tested well in the lab, and publish a short guide so staff can self-train.
Add inline help text to the fields of the existing screens, which needs no layout change and should leave experienced staff speed mostly intact.

rubric: An opt-in, shortcut-preserving rollout with cohort measurement protects expert throughput without retraining while improving learnability.
Distractors force abrupt change, fragment the product, or clutter screens in ways that can slow experts.
